subject: Science
title: Stem-cell decisions
reading_age_est: rough ARI grade 8.21 on 995 pupil-visible words; heuristic age guide 14.21 years, not a formal reading-age test
pupil_words: I am learning to weigh a possible benefit and risk of stem-cell research using evidence.
success_criteria: I can name a possible benefit and risk.
I can ask for evidence that tests a claim.
I can justify further research without claiming a cure.

vocab.definition: a cell that can divide and form specialised cell types
vocab.example: Stem cells are being studied for possible medical uses.
A possible benefit would be replacing damaged cells.

vocab.definition: a possible harmful result or uncertain effect
vocab.example: A study must consider a risk to volunteers.

vocab.definition: information that tests or supports a claim
vocab.example: The trial needs evidence of both benefit and harm.

retrieval.question: What is the name for a cell gaining a specialised job?
What two cells follow mitosis and cell splitting?
In which direction do particles spread by diffusion?
retrieval.answer: From a higher to a lower concentration overall.

worked_example.full: A fictional proposal may replace damaged cells. A possible harm is unknown. A careful study must measure both benefit and risk; possible use is not proven treatment.
worked_example.faded: Possible benefit: may replace damaged cells. Possible risk: ________. Evidence needed: a fair check of benefit and harm.
worked_example.removed_step: Identify an uncertain harmful result as a risk, without stating it has already happened.
worked_example.fade_next: Next time leave the evidence-needed column blank so the pupil decides what test or observation would discriminate a claim.

cfu.question: Show me: is “it might help” evidence that the treatment already works?
cfu.answer: No. It is a possible benefit; evidence from an appropriate study is needed.

hinge.question: A new fictional cell study reports improved movement but does not report harmful effects. Which review is justified?

options.text: A. The benefit can establish safety despite the missing report on harms.
options.diagnosis: Treats an observed benefit as proof of safety without harm data.

options.text: B. The missing report proves the study cannot have produced any benefit.
options.diagnosis: Treats missing harm reporting as proof that the reported benefit did not occur.

options.text: C. The improved movement proves the study will work for every person.
options.diagnosis: Generalises one study result to every person.

options.text: D. The benefit needs checking alongside missing risk evidence before a decision.

hinge.decision_rule: About 3 in 4 or more correct: proceed; otherwise re-model a fictional claim card beside an empty evidence column and ask the parallel hinge. No auto-grade.
hinge.parallel_hinge: Another fictional study reports harms but no benefit measure. Can it establish a favourable benefit-risk balance? Answer: no; both kinds of evidence are needed.

misconceptions.misconception: A reported benefit in one study proves a treatment will work for everyone.
misconceptions.spot: Pupil chooses C, claiming benefit for every person.
misconceptions.correction: Ask for further evidence of benefit across people and settings.

misconceptions.misconception: A reported benefit establishes safety without harm evidence.
misconceptions.spot: Pupil chooses A, treating benefit as proof of safety without harms data.
misconceptions.correction: Review benefits and missing risk evidence together before a decision.

we_do.support: Give three colour-coded headings and a fictional benefit/risk card; pupil supplies the missing risk and one request for evidence.
we_do.stretch: Ask whether “support more research” and “approve a treatment for use” require the same strength of evidence; justify the distinction.

tiers.F: Sort the fictional proposal statements under possible benefit, possible risk and evidence needed.
tiers.M: Explain why a proposal needs evidence of both effect and harm before a decision.
tiers.H: Evaluate whether to support further research with a qualified reason, risk and evidence request.

stems.F: A possible benefit is …; a possible risk is …
stems.M: The claim is not yet proven because we need evidence that …
stems.H: I would support/review further research if …; however, before treatment use I would need …

tiers.go_deeper: If a careful new study showed no improvement, how should the panel change its recommendation and why?
tiers.early_finisher: Separate further research from routine treatment; explain the evidence needed for each.

adaptations.cognition_learning: Scaffolding: Use benefit/risk/evidence columns with one completed model sentence, then hide one column cue.
adaptations.communication_interaction: Flexible grouping: Give a structured partner reply and a pass option; accept AAC, sign or spoken view of the fictional case.
adaptations.semh: Cognitive/metacognitive strategies: No request for personal belief or family medical history; private check-in, quiet alternative and regulated return.
adaptations.sensory_physical: Technology: Offer large text or immersive-reader-friendly fictional cards; pupil may speak or type the reason.
adaptations.eal: Explicit instruction: Define benefit, risk and evidence with concrete examples; allow planning in any language. Keep M and H scientific demand available.

speaking_frames: Speaking: “The proposal may …, but the evidence must show …”
Speaking: “I would recommend … because …; I would also check …”

ta_focus.i_do: “Which statement is a possible result, and which is measured evidence?”
ta_focus.we_do: “The risk column is blank. What question could the panel ask?”
ta_focus.independent: “What is your reason for more research or a pause? Which evidence would test it?”

prompt_ladder: Wait five seconds for the pupil to choose a column.
Point to a card heading and the last completed model sentence.
Ask “What would a careful panel need to find out?”
Model the first benefit card only; pupil places the risk card.
Place one card together, then invite a new evidence request independently.

F.q: What word means a possible good result?
What word means information used to test a claim?

M.q: Why is “might help” not proof of a treatment?
M.a: It states a possibility; evidence of benefit and risk must be collected.

M.q: Name one information request for the fictional study.
M.a: Ask for measured benefit or safety outcomes and how they were checked.

H.q: How could new evidence change a panel decision?
H.a: It could increase or reduce confidence about benefit and risk, changing whether further work is supported.

H.q: Why can further research be supported without approving routine treatment?
H.a: Research tests uncertainty under review; routine use needs stronger evidence of safety and benefit.

C. The improved movement proves the study will work for every person.
D. The benefit needs checking alongside missing risk evidence before a decision.
interactions.answer_key: D. The benefit needs checking alongside missing risk evidence before a decision. Teacher reads group response; no automatic grade.
